column4: The section explicitly sets this still-open question, أَلَمْ يَأْنِ, against the closed time of 89:23: the heart can soften to God's remembrance now, before remembrance becomes useless.
The section quotes this exact after-the-fact question: how can remembrance help them once a clear messenger has already come and been rejected?
The section quotes its question about what remembrance can do when the Hour arrives; it is the same boundary between warning time and recollection after arrival.
The quoted وَأَنَّىٰ لَهُمُ ٱلتَّنَاوُشُ مِن مَّكَانٍ بَعِيدٍ turns late belief into an impossible reach from far away, matching the section's hand reaching back for what has passed.
This is the section's closest parallel: on that day the human remembers what he strove for, just as the human remembers when Hell is brought in 89:23.
It completes 79:35 by making Hell plainly visible; the section's remembrance likewise occurs only when Hell has been brought into view.
The Great Overwhelming Event arrives immediately before the remembrance of 79:35, supplying the same catastrophic trigger that the brought-near Hell supplies in 89:23.
The section quotes the command that every soul inspect what it has sent ahead for tomorrow; it converts the regret of 89:24 into a present discipline.
A person sees what his hands sent ahead and the unbeliever says “if only”; judgment, prior deeds, and irreversible wishing coincide exactly as in 89:24.
The human is told what he sent ahead and left behind, directly unpacking the retrospective accounting inside قَدَّمْتُ.
Each soul comes to know what it sent ahead and left behind, joining the section's late knowledge to its image of provision dispatched in advance.
The wrongdoer bites his hands and wishes he had taken a path with the Messenger; this is another embodied “if only” after the path can no longer be chosen.
The recipient of the left-hand record wishes the record had never been given, the same judgment-day voice of belated desire that speaks in 89:24.
The section quotes ٱلدَّارَ ٱلْءَاخِرَةَ لَهِىَ ٱلْحَيَوَانُ to identify the Hereafter as life itself; it explains why the speaker can finally call that destination “my life.”
At death the speaker asks to be sent back, precisely the backward reach of one who now sees that something needed to be sent ahead.
He names the missing purpose—doing righteousness in what he left—but receives “No”; the verse closes the interval that 59:18 leaves open.
The section quotes God's taking souls at death and during sleep, then retaining one and sending another back; it makes the soul's departure and return as recurrent as breath until the fixed term.
The section quotes the angels' command أَخْرِجُوا أَنفُسَكُم and the humiliating recompense; forced extraction is the direct contrary scene to the tranquil soul being invited to return.
The section quotes the life-breath reaching the collarbones, fixing the soul image at the bodily threshold where return to ordinary life is ending.
The section quotes the day's driving toward the Lord; this compulsory destination sharpens the gentleness of “return to your Lord” addressed to the tranquil soul.
The section names this commanding soul as one state preceding tranquility; its impulse toward evil supplies one pole of the inner turbulence that has become still in 89:27.
The section names the self-reproaching soul as another state before tranquility, connecting conscience and retrospective blame without yet making remembrance too late.
The people of the Garden are told to eat and drink for what they sent before in past days; it is the fulfilled positive counterpart to wishing one had sent something ahead for life.
Hearts become tranquil through the remembrance of God; this verse directly joins the section's two key images, remembrance and the tranquil soul, while there is still time.
The one who turns from the Lord's signs forgets what his hands sent ahead; remembrance refused now and deeds encountered later are fused in one warning.
The bad companion led him away from the Reminder after it had come; it explains the missed opportunity behind the “if only” of 25:27.
During the angels' violent taking in 8:50, the punishment is identified as what their hands sent ahead; death-extraction and advance provision meet in one scene.
At the cosmic collapse every soul knows what it has brought with it, a close nonlexical parallel to the human's late remembrance of what should have been advanced.
The heedless person's covering is removed and sight becomes sharp on the judgment day; this is the same clarity arriving only after the chance to act has passed.
Every soul finds its good and evil deeds present and wishes the evil were far away; deeds made present and an impossible wish for distance reproduce the structure of 89:24.
قَدَمَ صِدْقٍ names a true precedence with the Lord, closely matching the dictionary sense of qadam as prior good sent on toward one's destination.
Whatever good people send ahead for themselves they will find with God; this is the direct present-tense answer to what the regretful human failed to send.
It repeats that whatever good people send ahead for themselves will be found with God, and thus gives the provision image an explicit destination.
God records both what people sent ahead and the traces they left, expanding the section's advance provision beyond the instant of death.
God says the warning had already been sent ahead; late argument fails because revelation itself arrived in advance of the encounter.
The right-hand recipient says he had expected to meet his account; timely anticipation produces the opposite speech from the left-hand recipient's surprise and regret.
فِى عِيشَةٍ رَّاضِيَةٍ places the foresighted person in a satisfying life, answering the section's question about which life deserved preparation.
The left-hand recipient wishes he had never known his account; it continues the judgment-day regret begun at 69:25 and specifies knowledge that arrives as misery.
His wish that death had been final exposes his discovery that death did not end life, the dark reverse of recognizing the Hereafter as the real life.
He discovers that his wealth has not availed him, tying belated regret to the section's earlier false reading of wealth as honor.
He discovers that his authority has vanished, completing the stripping away of the worldly measures by which he misread his life.
Standing over the Fire, the rejecters wish to be returned so they could believe; visible punishment produces exactly the section's too-late backward reach.
What they concealed becomes apparent, but the verse says a return would only repeat the rejection; it explains why their newly voiced wish cannot reopen action.
A soul says “alas” for what it neglected toward God after mocking; its regret identifies the earlier omission that 89:24 expresses as failure to send ahead.
The condemned soul claims it would have been mindful if guided, another judgment-time rewriting of a life whose guidance had already arrived.
On seeing punishment it asks for a return so it can become a doer of good, almost spelling out the work the speaker of 89:24 wishes had preceded him.
The reply recalls that God's signs did come but were denied; it locates the closed opportunity behind the wishes in 39:56–58.
The inhabitants of the Fire ask to be taken out so they can act righteously; the answer says they had enough life and a warner, making the missed span explicit.
The command to give before death is followed by a dying person's plea for a short delay to give and become righteous; it stages advance provision at the last breath.
God will not delay a soul when its term comes; this closes the time sought in 63:10 just as 89:23 closes the usefulness of remembrance.
Repentance is unavailable to one who waits until death and then says “now I repent”; it draws the precise boundary between an open and a closed act of return.
Faith at the arrival of the Lord's signs does not benefit a soul that neither believed nor earned good before; both belief and deed have a deadline.
The guilty lower their heads before their Lord, say they now see and hear, and ask to be returned to do right; certainty has come after agency has gone.
When the promised fulfillment comes, rejecters acknowledge the messengers and ask for intercession or a return to act differently; remembrance follows fulfillment too late.
The people of the Blaze say that listening or reasoning earlier would have kept them out; their recollection names the unused faculties of the missed life.
They confess their sin after the confession of 67:10, but the scene ends in exclusion rather than another chance.
When punishment arrives, wrongdoers ask for a brief postponement so they can answer the call and follow the messengers; their desired future is the past opportunity they lost.
On seeing punishment, the wrongdoers ask whether there is any way back; the question gives spatial form to the section's unreachable past.
As the true promise draws near, unbelievers stare and confess that they had been heedless; late awakening and the arrival of the threatened event coincide.
The unbelievers will wish they had submitted; this brief future scene distills the same identity-changing wish that comes only after the decisive boundary.
They do not believe until they see the painful punishment, making sight of the outcome the belated trigger for belief.
The punishment comes suddenly while they are unaware, explaining why the belief of 26:201 cannot become prior preparation.
Their first response is to ask for respite, another attempt to recover action time after the event has arrived.
Followers who see punishment wish for a return so they can disown their leaders; the desired reversal appears only when relationships and deeds have become visible.
The condemned wish for one return so they could become believers, a direct counterpart to wishing one had acted for the life now encountered.
With faces turned in the Fire, they wish they had obeyed God and the Messenger; the verse names the missed act from inside punishment.
The wrongdoer wishes he had not taken a particular person as intimate friend; it continues 25:27 by identifying the companionship behind the lost path.
The oath by the soul and the One who proportioned it presents the soul as a fashioned moral subject, the same subject later addressed as tranquil.
The soul is inspired with both its corruption and its mindfulness, supplying the opposing pressures whose resolution the tranquil soul represents.
Success belongs to one who purifies the soul, giving an enacted route toward the settled state addressed in 89:27.
Failure belongs to one who buries or corrupts the soul, the contrary moral development to its purification and tranquility.
One who fears standing before the Lord and restrains the soul from desire embodies the disciplined soul before its peaceful return.
The Garden becomes that person's refuge, directly anticipating the tranquil soul's invitation into God's Garden.
Angels descend on the steadfast, tell them not to fear or grieve, and announce the Garden; its consoling address closely parallels the address to the tranquil soul.
The Garden is presented as promised to every repeatedly returning, guarding person; prior return of the heart culminates in final return to the Lord.
The entrant feared the Merciful unseen and came with a returning heart, specifying the inward history behind the welcome of 50:32.
“Enter it in peace” and the day of permanence closely match the tranquil soul's invitation to enter the Garden and remain in true life.
Angels take the good while saying peace and telling them to enter the Garden for their deeds; it is a direct peaceful counterpart to the coerced extraction in 6:93.
The life-breath reaches the throat, recreating the bodily threshold described by the soul reaching the collarbones.
Those present can only look on while the departing life reaches the throat; human helplessness sharpens the impossibility of calling it back.
God is nearer to the dying person than the watchers, though they cannot see; the unseen Lord is already the soul's direction.
The challenge “bring it back” if humans are not subject to recompense makes the return of the departing soul explicitly impossible for them.
The passage then identifies the soul among those brought near, beginning the favorable destination corresponding to 89:27–30.
Rest, provision, and a Garden of bliss answer the tranquil soul's promised entrance with the same peaceful after-death outcome.
The angel of death takes people fully and then they are returned to their Lord; taking and return are the two motions joined in the section's soul image.
The stupor of death brings the truth the person was avoiding; unavoidable clarity at death anticipates the later remembrance when Hell is displayed.
At the collarbone threshold people ask who might heal or perform a saving rite; the question exposes the failed search for a way to keep the soul.
The dying person realizes this is separation, supplying the conscious recognition within the physical scene quoted at 75:26.
Leg is entwined with leg as departure completes; this bodily helplessness leads directly to the driving toward the Lord in 75:30.
The right-hand recipient openly invites others to read his record, the joyful reverse of the left-hand recipient wishing no record had been given.
A Garden speaker calls deliverance the great attainment, showing the realization of true life voiced from safety rather than regret at Hell.
“For the like of this let the workers work” turns knowledge of the lasting outcome into a present summons to prepare, the answer to “if only I had sent ahead.”
God created death and life to test which people are best in deed; life is the arena for sending action ahead, not the final measure of honor or humiliation.
Believers are told to answer God and the Messenger when called to what gives them life; timely response is the living opposite of remembrance after the call is over.
The command to remind when reminder benefits locates remembrance in its useful time, before the useless recollection of 89:23.
The one who fears will remember, showing the receptive person for whom warning becomes action rather than later regret.
The most wretched avoids that reminder, identifying the earlier refusal behind a later encounter with the Fire.
He enters the greatest Fire, the outcome that makes the rejected reminder concrete.
There he neither dies nor lives, a stark counterfeit of life beside the section's recognition that the Hereafter is the real life.
Those content and reassured by worldly life neglect the signs; their worldly اطمأنوا is the principal false counterpart to the soul tranquil before its Lord.
A person worships on an edge and becomes reassured only when worldly good arrives, exposing conditional comfort as the opposite of the settled soul after trial.
The unbelievers are driven in groups to Hell; this compulsory mass movement throws the singular, honoring summons to the tranquil soul into relief.
The mindful are conducted in groups to the Garden and welcomed by its keepers; alongside 89:27–30 it marks a distinct public form of blessed arrival.
Angels take souls while they are wronging themselves, and they try to offer submission at death; the forced, defensive scene reverses the tranquil soul's willing return.
They are ordered to enter Hell after their deathbed claim, the opposite destination and address from “enter My Garden.”
Angels strike faces and backs while taking the rejecters; violent taking provides the concrete reverse of the peaceful soul being called home.
What their souls sent ahead brings divine anger and lasting punishment, the negative counterpart to advance provision intended for true life.
They will never wish for death because of what their hands sent ahead; advance deeds here make the coming life feared rather than desired.
Hypocrites ask believers to wait and share light, but are told to go back and seek it; the command dramatizes a backward reach that can no longer recover provision.
They admit sharing the believers' former company, but are reminded that they delayed, doubted, and deceived themselves until God's command came.
No ransom is accepted that day, sealing the barrier erected after their failed attempt to go back for light.
Every soul tastes death and receives full reward later, while worldly life is deceptive enjoyment; the verse explicitly relocates life's true measure beyond death.
People prefer the nearer worldly life, identifying the misplaced preference that the regretful speaker corrects only at judgment.
The Hereafter is better and more enduring, explaining why preparation belongs to that life rather than the preferred nearer one.
People love the immediate life, a temporal attachment that explains why they fail to send ahead.
They leave the Hereafter aside; paired with 75:20, this is the exact misplacement reversed by “for my life.”
People love the immediate world and leave behind a heavy day; what they treat as distant becomes the day on which advance provision matters.
Their terror and seizure from a near place introduce the impossible reach of 34:52; nearness of capture contrasts with the distance of recovery.
They had disbelieved earlier and cast claims at the unseen from far away; it explains why the later attempt to reach belief is itself now distant.
A barrier is placed between them and what they desire, completing the section's image of a hand extended toward something no longer attainable.
Those mindful remember when a satanic suggestion touches them and then see clearly; it is an in-life version of remembrance that still repairs sight.
Hard hearts are warned for resisting God's remembrance, identifying the condition that must soften before late remembrance becomes futile.
Skins and hearts soften at God's remembrance while hearing revelation; bodily response now contrasts with recollection only after Hell appears.
The Quran is called a reminder, locating the material for remembrance before the final scene.
Whoever wills may remember it; the open invitation clarifies the agency no longer available in 89:23.
Remembrance remains under God's will, adding dependence and fear to the present opportunity without reopening the later one.
The revelation is characterized as a reminder, the available object that can be taken up before recollection turns retrospective.
Whoever wills may remember it; the voluntary present stance is specifically what the late rememberer can no longer occupy.
Revelation is a reminder for one who fears; fear receives the message before the judgment scene instead of being generated by it.
The Prophet is told to remind with the Quran whoever fears the threat, pairing present warning with the future threat that makes remembrance too late.
The command to remind because reminder benefits believers states the useful function whose expiration the section dramatizes.
Punishment is attributed to what their hands sent ahead, using the section's provision verb for a harmful store laid up by one's own action.
A calamity reaches them because of what their hands sent ahead; consequences make prior deeds return to their doers even before the final account.
Hell's punishment is said to be for what the person's hands sent ahead, giving the brought Fire an individualized history.
A calamity caused by what hands sent ahead would prompt a plea for a messenger; God sends warning beforehand, removing that late excuse.
People despair when evil touches them because of what their hands sent ahead, showing advance action returning as experienced consequence.
People exult in mercy yet despair at adversity caused by what their hands sent ahead, echoing the section's critique of reading changing provision as honor or humiliation.
Followers in Hell tell their leaders “you brought this upon us”; قَدَّمْتُمُوهُ gives advance causation a communal and accusatory form.
“Send ahead for yourselves” uses the same imperative of prior provision; its immediate marital context makes the precise good intended less explicit than in 2:110.
When his garden is ruined, its owner wrings his hands and wishes he had not associated anyone with his Lord; worldly loss rehearses the section's sequence from false security to regret.
Everyone is presented and no secret remains hidden; this exposure supplies the shared courtroom setting for the two opposed records and speeches that follow.
The people in the Fire blame the leaders and great ones who led them from the path, specifying the social history behind the wish in 33:66.
They ask for doubled punishment and curse upon those leaders; regret has become accusation, but still cannot alter their own prior obedience.
At last the person wishes for an east-to-west distance from the misleading companion; judgment reveals the relationship's true cost only after separation is impossible.
Pharaoh's belief at drowning is answered with “Now?”; the temporal rebuke is a sharp earlier instance of recognition arriving beyond its useful moment.
The condemned acknowledge two deaths and two lives and ask whether there is a way out; multiplied life does not supply another opportunity once guilt is confessed.
The Garden speaker asks whether the blessed will die again, opening a recognition that the first death has led into enduring life.
He specifies that only the first death occurs and no further punishment follows, clarifying the permanence celebrated in 37:60.
Worldly life is play and diversion while the afterlife abode is better for the mindful; this is a concise correction of life's misplaced name and value.
Those content with worldly life over the Hereafter are told its enjoyment is little, explaining the preference that leaves the later life unprovisioned.
Those who prefer worldly life over the Hereafter bend away from God's way; their temporal preference becomes a path away from the destination.
Their rejection is traced to preferring worldly life over the Hereafter, a direct reason for failing to prepare for the life encountered after death.
The worldly life is temporary enjoyment and the Hereafter the abiding home; “home” gives the tranquil soul's return a durable destination.
Worldly goods are temporary enjoyment while what is with God is better and more lasting, distinguishing present allotment from stored destination.
Worldly life passes through play, display, wealth, growth, and decay before the Hereafter; its sequence explains why present abundance cannot define one's lasting life.
Abraham asks how the dead are revived so that his heart may become reassured; tranquility here is settled certainty about restored life.
Divine aid is made good news so hearts may be reassured; this occurrence shows tranquility arising from trust rather than possession.
The disciples seek a sign so their hearts may be reassured and they may know the truth; it offers a questioning, evidential shade of the tranquil state.
The promised angelic aid is given so hearts may be reassured; inward settlement is tied to God's support amid fear.
A heart remaining tranquil in faith under coercion distinguishes inward settled life from words forced outward.
Those who say their Lord is God and remain upright have no fear or grief, the stable moral posture echoed in the address to the tranquil soul.
They are companions of the Garden because of what they did, connecting that stable posture to the same final entrance.
“My servants, no fear upon you today, nor shall you grieve” is another direct divine welcome on the final day.
The addressees are identified as those who believed in the signs and submitted, supplying the lived response behind the peaceful address.
They are told to enter the Garden rejoicing, closely paralleling the tranquil soul's movement from personal address to admission.
The greatest terror does not grieve the righteous, and angels greet them with their promised day; peaceful reception stands within the same final catastrophe.
Every soul is held in pledge for what it earned; the soul's final condition is inseparable from the provision made by its own deeds.
The person is told to read his own record and that his own soul suffices as accountant; judgment turns the self into witness of its prior life.
Every soul comes with a driver and a witness, contrasting the universal compelled procession with the intimate direct call to the tranquil soul.
Every soul tastes death and is tested by good and evil before being returned; trial, death, and return are placed in a single arc.
Every soul tastes death and is then returned to God, giving the section's command “return” its universal background.
The dawn “when it breathes” uses the literal exhalation sense from which the section derives nafs, projecting the inward-outward motion onto the morning.
Immediately after the call for hearts to soften, God says He gives life to the earth after its death; it leaves open the possibility of revival before the fixed end.
Earth revived after death becomes evidence that God will revive the dead, moving the word life from growth to resurrection as the section's dictionary range does.
One who was dead is given life and light to walk among people; it supplies a moral-intellectual sense of life before bodily resurrection.
The invoked beings are dead, not living, and unaware of resurrection; life, perception, and awareness are separated just as the section's lexical account distinguishes powers of life.
